abstract:
A new method called Superb-seq pairs Cas9 editing with single-cell RNA sequencing to show which edits, including off-target ones, occur in each cell and how they alter gene expression, offering a clearer view of genome editing’s potential consequences.

The post Single-Cell Method Reveals On- and Off-Target Effects of Cas9 Edits on Gene Expression appeared first on GEN - Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology News.

metadata.author: Uduak Thomas

content.value:
Scientists at the Salk Institute and their collaborators have published a paper in Nature Methods describing Superb-seq, a method of reading out both on and off target edits made by CRISPR/Cas9 technology. According to the developers, the tool makes it possible to read changes made by CRISPR at single-cell resolution to identify unwanted edits and assess how those edits change gene activity. Their paper is titled “Joint single-cell capture of Cas9 edits and transcriptomes reveals on- and off-target effects on gene expression.” 

“What really inspired Superb-seq was a frustration with the existing state of affairs,” said Graham McVicker, PhD, senior author of the study and an associate professor at Salk. “We knew there were problems with CRISPR making unwanted edits, but also there was no good way to see what those edits were and how they affected the cell—what we wanted to see was invisible using current technologies.”

According to the developers, Superb-seq is able to show where unwanted edits are located as well as how those edits disrupt key genes that protect against unhealthy cellular states. Specifically, Superb-seq integrates Cas9 editing, T7 transcription, and single-cell RNA sequencing to capture single-cell edits and their impact on gene expression. The team has tested it on 34,000 cells from three different cell lines. “There are some people that have worked on this off-target issue before that have an awareness of how bad it is, but for many people that pick up CRISPR to use in the lab, the extent of this problem will really come as a surprise,” McVicker said. “I knew off-targets were an issue, but they were far more frequent than I was expecting.”

Using seven guide RNAs to target genes in one group of 10,000 human leukemia cells grown in the lab, Superb-seq detected 43 edit sites, including 36 of which were off-target, and 5,761 edited cells. Additionally, Superb-seq detected gene expression changes caused by genome edits that are invisible to existing edit detection methods. It also improved interpretation of the effect of edits compared to Perturb-seq, which reads out gene expression and guide RNAs but not the resulting edits.

The Salk scientists anticipate that Superb-seq could support applications in basic research, drug development, and personalized medicine. For existing studies that have used CRISPR to study different aspects of biology, “Superb-seq could reveal the extent to which off-target edits color all those findings,” said Michael Lorenzini, PhD, one of the first authors on the paper and a staff scientist in McVicker’s lab. Beyond basic discovery, “our tool could be immensely helpful in establishing the safety of genome therapy candidates early on in development. Superb-seq could be used to profile candidates and learn what their off-target edits are, as well as their effects,” he added. 

The team also envisions Superb-seq as a valuable tool for generating training data to improve the accuracy of machine learning models of cellular function. McVicker, Lorenzini, and another co-author, Brad Balderson, PhD, have filed a patent for Superb-seq.
